title: The shrinking map

data.source: Banach (1922), Hutchinson (1981), Letac (1986), Diaconis and Freedman (1999); cited from memory. Computed and simulated, seeded.

prediction: The flat seed map shrinks distances by exactly q, so by Banach's theorem it has one fixed point and forgets its start as q^n; memory is a geometric series; swapping two marks changes the seed by (1 - q)^2 (B - A); and on a circle the map is not a contraction at the point opposite the mark.
baseline: Banach's fixed-point theorem (1922); iterated random maps (Hutchinson 1981; Letac 1986; Diaconis and Freedman 1999). Decoy: a running mean, for which order does not matter.
relation: identical on flat content; on a circle the hypothesis of the theorem fails at the far point
status_line: CRR here is: a renaming of a contraction map with rate q (Banach), with memory as a geometric series; on a circle the theorem's condition fails at the far point, as R5 already warns.
why: R5's flat seed rule (Phoenix status ASSUMPTION) is a contraction with rate q, so its fixed point, its forgetting, its geometric-series memory and its long-run spread all follow from Banach's theorem and the theory of iterated random maps. The order of marks matters by (1 - q)^2 (B - A), as the colloquy found. On a circle the step tears at the point opposite the mark and is not a contraction there, which is the case R5 guards against by asking for a convex content domain.
